messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol had been working late in the incident-response room when the confrontation began in the parking lot outside her office. A man from a neighboring building, already agitated, came toward her with something in his hand that she only registered at first as a weapon-like shape; the motion was sudden, the shouting close enough to hear through the glass. In the scramble that followed, Marisol acted on panic and certainty that someone was about to be hurt. She shoved him away with force, he fell badly against the concrete and sustained a serious injury, and the memory of that night never settled into a clean story afterward. What stayed with her was the sight of him going down, the sound of impact, and then the shock of realizing that her own action had done this. Since her husband’s death years earlier, she had already been living with a kind of private grief, but this was different: she described it as a wound of guilt, the feeling that she had crossed some line she could never uncross.

In the weeks after the incident, Marisol began to notice that when she remembered the event she was flooded by overwhelming grief before she could even picture it clearly. Sometimes the emotion arrived without any image at all, a hard surge in her chest and stomach that left her nauseated and shaking; at other times she tried to pull the scene back together and found that there were parts she simply could not remember no matter how hard she tried. That blankness frightened her almost as much as the memory itself. She had come to believe that if she could only reconstruct the missing pieces, she would know whether she had been reckless, whether she had used too much force, whether she had missed a chance to stop before it was too late. Instead, the gaps kept her stuck with the worst possibility, and each attempt to fill them in only made the grief feel more immediate and more unbearable.

The strangest part, Marisol said, was how easily the memory could be stirred by things that seemed ordinary to other people. Weapons or objects used as weapons were the fastest route back: a screwdriver on a workbench, a wrench in a garage, even the black edge of a tool in a kitchen drawer could make her body tense before she had time to think. Confrontations had the same effect. If two coworkers raised their voices in a meeting, or if she saw an argument unfold in a grocery store parking lot, the scene from that night would flare inside her, and with it the same grief and uncertainty. She did cybersecurity analysis from home three days a week now, but even the office could feel unsafe; she found herself scanning entrances, noting who was standing too close to whom, and rehearsing how quickly a harmless disagreement could become physical. Her fear was not only that another confrontation might lead to injury, but that it would drag her back into the same emotional flood and the same missing fragments she could not master.

Over time, Marisol began arranging her life around avoiding those moments. She stopped walking past the side lot at work and started coming in through the loading dock if she had to go in at all. She turned down after-hours team dinners because bars and crowded sidewalks made unexpected conflict feel too close. At home she kept her eyes away from the kitchen drawer where the big tools were stored, and when a movie or news report showed a weapon, she would leave the room. These choices made sense to her: if she could keep weapons, trauma-related events, and confrontations out of reach, maybe she could keep the grief from breaking open again. But the avoidance narrowed her world. She became more isolated from colleagues, less likely to linger after meetings, and more dependent on carefully controlled routines that left little room for spontaneity or comfort.

By the time she sought help, Marisol was exhausted by how tightly the memory and the triggers seemed to chase one another. A tool handle, a heated exchange, even a story on the evening news about a violent incident could pull her back into the night at the office, and then the grief would rise so fast that she would flee, shut down, or spend hours trying to force the scene into order. The more she tried to make sense of what she had done, the more the missing pieces seemed to mock her, and the more she feared she might be one accident away from becoming that person again. What finally brought her in was the realization that her world had become organized around not being reminded, and that the cost was growing too high. She wanted relief from the flood of grief and from the constant watching for danger, but what she feared most was that if she stopped avoiding, she would be overwhelmed by the same unbearable memory and never come back from it.
